the position title, telephone number, postal address and email address of a contact person for requests to access and correct personal information. An APP entity could establish a generic telephone number and email address that will not change with staff movements (for example privacy@agency.gov.au). [6]
1.24 If an APP entity wishes an individual to follow a particular procedure in requesting access to or correction of their personal information, the entity could publish that procedure and draw attention to it, for example, by providing a link in the entity’s APP Privacy Policy. However, an APP entity cannot require the individual to follow a particular procedure to make the access or correction request (see Chapter 12 (APP 12) and Chapter 13 (APP 13)).
1.25 An agency’s APP Privacy Policy could also refer to the Freedom of Information Act 1982 (FOI Act) and explain that the access and correction requirements in the Privacy Act operate alongside and do not replace other informal or legal procedures by which an individual can be provided with access to, or correction of, their personal information, including the FOI Act (this is discussed in more detail in Chapter 12 (APP 12) and Chapter 13 (APP 13)).

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
1.26 An APP entity may have other specific access or correction obligations outside the Privacy Act (for example the Consumer Data Right under Part IVD of the Competition and Consumer Act 2010). In such cases, the APP entity could also refer or explain those obligations where appropriate.
1.27 An APP Privacy Policy must explain how an individual can complain about an APP entity’s breach of the APPs or a binding registered APP code (APP 1.4(e)). It is implicit in this requirement that an entity which is bound by a binding, registered APP code should clearly state that fact and name the code.
1.28 Details that should also be included in the APP Privacy Policy are the procedure and contact details for complaining directly to the APP entity (see for example, the generic contact details in paragraph 1.22) and, where applicable, the procedure for complaining to an external complaint body (such as an external dispute resolution scheme of which the entity is a member and that is recognised by the Information Commissioner). [7] The policy could inform individuals of the different stages in complaint handling: in most cases, a complaint should first be made in writing to the entity, as required by s 40(1A), and that the entity should be given a reasonable time (usually 30 days) to respond; following engagement with the entity, a complaint may be taken to a recognised external dispute resolution scheme of which the entity is a member; and, after those avenues have been considered, a complaint may be taken to the OAIC.
1.29 The policy could refer to other complaint avenues that operate alongside the Privacy Act. For example, banks are required to provide information to customers about complaint handling and dispute resolution in relation to the bank’s obligations under the Corporations Act 2001, the Code of Banking Practice, and the Electronic Funds Transfer Code of Conduct. In these circumstances, the APP Privacy Policy could note the different procedures for privacy and non-privacy complaints (or link to other explanatory material the APP entity has published).
1.30 An APP Privacy Policy must set out whether personal information is likely to be disclosed to overseas recipients and the countries in which such recipients are likely to be located ‘if it is practicable to specify those countries in the policy’ (APP 1.4(f) and 1.4(g)). This includes a likely disclosure to a related body corporate located overseas, and the country in which that body is located. An APP entity can be regarded as likely to disclose personal information to an overseas recipient if it is the entity’s current practice or it has established plans to do so.

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
1.31 An APP entity is required to set out in the policy only likely disclosures of personal information to overseas recipients, and not likely uses of personal information by the entity. For example, routing personal information, in transit, through a server located outside Australia would usually be considered a ‘use’. [8] Similarly, it would also be a use and not a disclosure for an entity to make personal information accessible to an overseas office of the entity, such as a consular office. [9] For further discussion of the requirements applying to a cross-border disclosure of personal information, and what is considered a disclosure, see Chapter 8 (APP 8).
1.32 An example of when it may be impracticable to specify the countries in which overseas recipients of personal information are likely to be located is where personal information is likely to be disclosed to numerous overseas recipients and the burden of determining where those recipients are likely to be located is excessively time-consuming, costly or inconvenient in all the circumstances. However, an APP entity is not excused from specifying the countries by reason only that it would be inconvenient, time-consuming or impose some cost to do so. As in other examples, it is the responsibility of the entity to be able to justify that this is impracticable.
1.33 If personal information is disclosed to numerous overseas locations, one practical option may be to list those countries in an appendix to the APP Privacy Policy rather than in the body of the policy. Another option in these circumstances may be to include a link in the APP Privacy Policy to a regularly updated list of those countries, accessible from the APP entity’s website. Where it is not practicable to specify the countries, the entity could instead identify general regions (such as European Union countries).
1.34 This requirement to describe overseas disclosure practices in an APP Privacy Policy complements the obligation on an APP entity under APP 5.2(j) and (i) to notify an individual when personal information is being collected if the personal information is likely to be disclosed to overseas recipients and the location of those recipients (see Chapter 5 (APP 5)).

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
1.35 From 10 December 2026, APP 1.7 requires APP entities to include the information outlined in APP 1.8 in their APP Privacy Policy if:
the entity has arranged for a computer program to make, or do a thing that is substantially and directly related to making a decision (APP 1.7(a)); and
the decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual (APP 1.7(b)); and
personal information about the individual is used in the operation of the computer program to make the decision or do the thing that is substantially and directly related to making the decision (APP 1.7(c)).
1.36 APP 1.8 outlines the information which must be included in an entity’s APP Privacy Policy if the conditions in APP 1.7 are met. This includes:
the kinds of personal information used in the operation of such computer programs; and
the kinds of such decisions made solely by the operation of such computer programs; and
the kinds of such decisions for which a thing, that is substantially and directly related to making the decision, is done by the operation of such computer programs.
1.37 For the purposes of APP 1.7 and 1.8, APP 1.9 states that:
making a decision includes refusing or failing to make a decision; and
doing a thing includes refusing or failing to do a thing; and
a decision may affect the rights or interests of an individual, whether the rights or interests of the individual are adversely or beneficially affected.
1.38 The decisions must be a decision that ‘could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual (APP 1.7(b)).
1.39 As APP 1.9 sets out, the meaning of ‘decision’ is broad and can be something an entity chooses to do or chooses not to do. These include:
making a decision – choosing to take an action or not take an action
doing something – including deliberately doing something or failing/refusing to do something
a decision that affects a person – where the outcome could reasonably be expected to benefit or disadvantage that individual.
1.40 For the avoidance of doubt, where a human decision-maker has made the decision, or done a thing related to making the decision, and has used a computer program for purposes other than facilitating the decision-making (such as using a word processing program to document a decision), this will not be captured. [10]

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
Example A: Glowride, a rideshare company, uses a computer program to analyse customer’s personal information to manage the customer’s ongoing usage of the service, including feedback or payment data or ratings provided by ride share drivers. One of the actions the computer program can execute is to suspend a user’s account.
While a decision to suspend a customer’s account may have a relatively minor impact on some customers, for a customer experiencing vulnerability who relies on Glowride to attend medical appointments, access essential services or maintain employment, the decision could significantly affect their rights or interests.
The example demonstrates that for a decision to be one that could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual, it will depend on the individual’s circumstances (such as a child or a person experiencing vulnerability). The effects of a decision must be more than trivial and must have the potential to significantly influence the circumstances of the individual concerned.
1.41 Other examples of the kinds of decisions that may affect the rights or interests of an individual include: [11]
a decision made under a provision of an Act or a legislative instrument to grant, or to refuse to grant, a benefit to the individual. For example, this may include a decision in relation to granting admission to a country or entitlement to a housing benefit.
a decision that affects the individual’s rights under a contract, agreement or arrangement. For example, this may include a contract for a life insurance policy.
a decision that affects the individual’s access to a significant service or support. For example, this may include access to healthcare services.
Importantly, a decision may be within scope of the APP 1.7-1.9 transparency obligation even where a computer program output does not replace the entire decision-making process or is subject to human review.
1.42 APP 1.7(a) uses the wording, ‘the entity has arranged for a computer program’.
1.43 The words ‘arranged for’ clarify that it is the entity responsible for arranging the computer program to make, or do a thing that is substantially and directly related to making, a decision, which must meet the requirements in APP 1.7. ( Example B and C )

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
1.44 This recognises that a computer program may be operated by one entity, but another entity is responsible for arranging for the computer program to make, or do a thing that is substantially and directly related to making, a decision. ( Example D )
Example B: An employer permits or directs employees to use an artificial intelligence (AI) chat tool to draft performance assessments that determine promotion decisions.
Example C: An entity contracts a third-party software company to automatically approve or decline refunds on its behalf.
Example D: The National Taxation Authority (NTA) uses a third-party software called EzyTax to consider individual applications for their eligibility for a tax refund. EzyTax automatically approves or rejects the applications on behalf of the NTA depending on the personal information provided by the individual. The NTA has arranged for the EzyTax software to make decisions on its behalf.
The OAIC generally expects that the APP 1.7-1.9 transparency obligation typically remains with the APP entity who is using personal information to make a decision or do a thing that significantly affects the rights or interests of an individual.
1.45 APP entities should actively identify, assess and keep oversight over the third-party computer programs that they use to make a decision, both during and after procurement. Amongst other considerations, entities should understand how a computer program is being used in a third-party product or service to make or assist decisions and what types of decisions are being made. In this regard, APP entities and third-party computer program providers should ensure their contractual arrangements are clear regarding which entity maintains ultimate decision-making capability or judgement.
Privacy Tip: APP entities should be aware of the impact of any contractual arrangements they have with other entities when considering their APP 1.7 obligations. APP entities may still be required to comply with APP 1.7 where they have a contractual arrangement in place with another entity who provides them with a computer program.
The OAIC outlines below a non-exhaustive list of examples that would generally be considered ‘arranged for’ for the purposes of the APP 1.7-1.9 transparency obligation:
an entity procures another entity’s AI system to screen and rank job applications leading to a decision being made on who to employ

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
an employer permits or directs employees to use an AI chat tool to draft performance assessments that determine promotion decisions
an entity contracts a third-party software company to automatically approve or decline refunds on its behalf
an entity has a case management system that automatically escalates particular types of complaints.
1.46 The meaning of computer program is intended to be interpreted broadly.
1.47 The term ‘computer program’ is intended to take its ordinary meaning and encompass a broad range of matters, including pre-programmed rule-based processes, artificial intelligence and machine learning processes to make a computer execute a task. [12]
A wide range of technologies are likely to fall within the definition of computer program, including commonly-used software, apps, or word-processing tools. Generative AI tools used to generate text, images, videos, code or synthesis, including chatbots and other types of AI all fall within the definition of computer program for the purpose of the APP 1.7-1.9 transparency obligation.
1.48 Under APP 1.7, an APP Privacy Policy must contain the information outlined in APP 1.8 if, amongst other things, the entity has arranged for a computer program to make, or do a thing that is substantially and directly related to making a decision (APP 1.7(a)).
1.49 The use of the words ‘do a thing that is substantially and directly related to making a decision’ in APP 1.7(a) reflects that a computer program may be used to recommend a decision to a human decision-maker or guide a human decision-maker. [13]
1.50 Where a computer program is used to recommend a decision to a human decision-maker, or guide a human decision-maker, the thing must be substantially and directly related to making a decision to be captured:
substantially means where it is a key factor in facilitating the human’s decision making
directly means where the thing has a direct connection with making the decision. [14]
1.51 In addition, the OAIC considers that substantial means ‘real or of substance and not insubstantial or nominal’. [15]
1.52 A computer program may be substantially and directly related to making a decision regardless of whether the nature of the output is advisory or determinative. When considering if an advisory output is within scope of this limb of the APP 1.7-1.9 transparency obligation, APP entities should consider factors including:

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
which part of the decision-making process the computer program was used for
the sources of information used to generate the output
the parameters provided to the computer program to generate a decision
how the computer program output ultimately influenced the human decision-maker’s judgement.
1.53 An APP entity may consider this non-exhaustive list of factors to enable it to assess whether a computer program substantially facilitates and is directly connected to a human decision-maker's decision:
degree of reliance on the computer program output ( Example E ) for example, the higher the reliance, the higher the likelihood of the computer program output being determinative rather than advisory
for example, the higher the reliance, the higher the likelihood of the computer program output being determinative rather than advisory
ability and likelihood of human override over a computer program output ( Example F )
nature of the output (advisory vs determinative) ( Example G )
transparency and explainability of outputs available to the decision-maker (what the computer program did and why) ( Example H )
integration and complexity of the computer program into the decision-making workflow ( Example I ).
Example E: A bank uses a computer program to assess loan applications. The loan officer relies heavily on the computer program’s risk score and almost always follows its recommendation.
Example F: An online marketplace uses a computer program to suspend seller accounts if commission payments are not made by a seller within 60 days. Staff can overturn the algorithm’s decision, however, because the computer program is considered highly accurate, staff rarely overturn the algorithm’s decision.
Example G: A private tertiary education institute uses a computer program to rank scholarship applications. The computer program produces a recommendation, however, the scholarship panel makes the final decision and can disregard the ranking. The recommendation produced by the computer program is substantially and directly related to making a decision as the scholarship panel considers the ranking provided by the computer program even though they may choose to ignore it.
Example H: An insurance company uses a computer program to determine whether a claim should be rejected. The system provides the claims officer with a rejection decision but does not explain which information led to the outcome.

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
Example I: A rental company uses a computer program that automatically collects an applicant’s information, calculates a suitability score and places the result directly into the employee’s application assessment screen. The system is deeply integrated into the decision-making process.
1.54 The examples provided above demonstrate that a computer program does not necessarily need to make the final decision or to be the only decision-maker for a type of decision. An output can still substantially facilitate and be directly connected to a human decision where the human decision maker relies on or is significantly influenced by the computer program’s output.
1.55 Under APP 1.7, APP privacy policies must contain the information outlined in APP 1.8 if, amongst other things, the decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual (APP 1.7(b)).
1.56 APP 1.9(c) outlines that a decision may affect the rights or interests of an individual, whether the rights or interests of the individual are adversely or beneficially affected.
1.57 Significantly means the impact of the decision or thing must be more than trivial and must have the potential to considerably influence the circumstances or outcomes for the individual concerned.
1.58 The circumstances of an individual may influence whether or not a decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of the individual, such as in the case of a child or vulnerable person.
1.59 In determining whether a decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual, APP entities should consider adverse effects on rights and interests.
1.60 A right is a moral or legal entitlement to have or be able to do something. [16] Australian law grants many legal rights which reflect human rights found in customary law, the Australian Constitution, statute law, common law, and international treaties to which Australia is a party. Rights afforded to Australians under these sources of law include:
social and economic rights (e.g. housing, food, sanitation, healthcare, education, etc.)
civil and political rights (e.g. freedom of movement and assembly, freedom of expression, etc.)
1.61 An interest refers to a concern, benefit, stake or claim relating to something. In the context of the APP 1.7-1.9 transparency obligation, APP entities may consider a range of interests including legal, personal liberty, status, preservation of livelihood, personal and commercial reputation, property, employment, health, immigration, financial, commercial, behaviour choices and a child’s interest in the provision of a supportive, safe and secure home. [17]

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
1.62 Other factors APP entities may consider when determining the likelihood that a decision could affect an individual’s rights or interest may include the sensitive nature of the information used, whether they are dealing with vulnerable persons, whether there are any intrusive practices being used by the APP entity and if there are any significant financial outcomes involved.
1.63 The following examples of a decision ‘could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual’: [18]
a decision made under a provision of an Act or a legislative instrument to grant, or to refuse to grant, a benefit to the individual. For example, this may include a decision in relation to granting admission to a country or entitlement to a housing benefit
a decision that affects the individual’s rights under a contract, agreement or arrangement. For example, this may include a contract for a life insurance policy
a decision that affects the individual’s access to a significant service or support. For example, this may include access to healthcare services
the use of computer programs to target individuals with content and advertisements may have a significant effect on an individual if, for example, it results in differential and/or personalised pricing for provision of, or access to, significant goods or services, or limits access to employment opportunities.
Example F: Life Insured is a life insurance company that has recently started to use an automated decision-making (ADM) software that has decreased employees’ time for considering individual applications. The software being used allows employees to enter applicants’ personal information and receive a decision of whether to approve or decline their life insurance policy in as little as 10 seconds. Although this software has improved the efficiency of Life Insured, they now must update their APP Privacy Policy to comply with APP 1.7 due to the software being used having a significant effect on the rights and interests of an individual.
1.64 The circumstances of an individual may also influence whether or not a decision could reasonably be expected to significantly affect the rights or interests of the individual, such as in the case of a child or vulnerable person. The effects must be more than trivial and must have the potential to significantly influence the circumstances of the individual concerned.

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
1.65 Whether a person is a child or experiencing vulnerability is relevant, to the extent that a decision may have a greater impact on that person, as opposed to a person who is not a child or is not experiencing vulnerability. For example, a decision’s effect on a child, individual from a low socio-economic background, Indigenous Australian, or person with a disability may be considered significant compared to its effect on other individuals.
1.66 When assessing vulnerability, APP entities should consider whether the decision in question produces an output that is materially different for a vulnerable cohort of individuals when compared to the general Australian population. Where this is the case, the computer program’s decision should be taken to significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual.
The OAIC outlines below a non-exhaustive list of significant rights or interests that would generally be considered in scope of the obligation:
access to essential food and nutrition
access to healthcare, emergency or aged care services (including ‘in home’ services)
access to physical assistance or support
financial assistance
access to educational services
access to essential banking and credit services
access to telecommunications
access to essential utilities
access to employment opportunities
access to housing.
1.67 To ensure compliance with APP 1.7, APP entities must strike a balance between providing enough meaningful information for individuals to understand their use of a computer program and avoiding excessive detail that obscures the purpose of transparency and clear communication.
Privacy Tip: Commercial-in-confidence information about automated decision-making systems is excluded from the requirement of APP 1.7. [19] In this regard, the APP 1.7-1.9 transparency obligation does not require APP entities to include information in APP 1 privacy policies that is commercially sensitive information or would expose trade secrets.
The OAIC notes that in considering whether information is commercial-in-confidence, APP entities should classify information as falling in this category only if its release could harm an APP entity’s commercial interests. The exclusion in APP 1.7 applies to the narrower category of ‘commercial-in-confidence’ information rather than information that has ‘commercial value’.
For example, an APP entity may have a genuine financial interest in using a computer program to handle personal information to make decisions that significantly affect the rights or interests of an individual but would not be able to apply the commercial-in-confidence exclusion because the use of the program itself does not expose sensitive operational information about the entity.

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
1.68 Entities must ensure that meaningful and accessible information is provided to individuals.
1.69 Entities should strike an appropriate balance to ensure information is:
articulated clearly and in plain language and easy to understand
structured to enable consumers to request further information, where required
appropriately tailored – sufficiently specific to be meaningful, while avoiding overwhelming levels of detail
organised so similar information is grouped in a logical manner
framed in a way that allows the information and the decision to be challenged or contested.
1.70 In complying with the APP 1.7-1.9 transparency obligation, APP entities may group information about the categories of decisions and types of personal information in their privacy policy to comply with the transparency obligation. However, the level of detail provided about these processes must be meaningful to a reasonable person.
1.71 Where an APP entity chooses to group information about categories of decisions and types of personal information used to inform a decision, this should be considered with regard to the sensitivity of the information relied upon by the computer program. Privacy policies should be able to clearly articulate where more sensitive types of information (e.g. health information or biometric templates) are used in the making of a computer’s decision.
1.72 In circumstances where all decisions made by an entity rely on the use of the same type of personal information, APP entities are not required to separate out each decision on a granular basis in their privacy policy but should still consider presenting the information in ways that assist an individual’s understanding.
1.73 For example, an APP entity may use a range of different computer programs for fraud detection, scam identification, and cybersecurity which may prevent access to significant goods or services. In this case, an APP privacy policy may outline it uses a range of fraud prevention technologies which process an individual’s personal information (e.g. identity information, geolocation data, biometric information, and IP addresses) to decode whether to permit, flag or deny access to an account with the APP entity.
Government agencies’ disclosure obligations under the Information Publication Scheme (IPS)
1.74 All Government agencies that are subject to the FOI Act are required to comply with obligations of disclosure under the Information Publication Scheme (IPS).

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Information that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy
1.75 That obligation extends to publishing a plan showing how an agency will comply with the IPS and as well as information that sets out what the agency does, the way it does it, and operational information. ADM information, that assists an agency to perform or exercise its functions or powers in making decisions or recommendations that affect the public, should be proactively published under the IPS.
1.76 Government agencies may consider cross linking IPS disclosures regarding ADM information with their APP 1.7 disclosure obligation.
1.77 Part 13 of the FOI Guidelines issued under section 93A of the FOI Act that agencies and ministers must have regard to when exercising a function or power provide further information on the IPS and associated considerations with the use of ADM systems and artificial intelligence.

APP 1 — Developing an APP Privacy Policy > Other matters for inclusion in an APP Privacy Policy
1.79 The list of matters that must be included in an APP Privacy Policy, as discussed above, is not exhaustive. In all cases, the policy should contain sufficient information to describe how the APP entity manages personal information.
1.80 The following are examples of other information that could be included:
any exemptions under the Privacy Act that apply to personal information held by the entity or to any of its acts or practices
whether the APP entity retains a record of personal information about all individuals (or categories of persons) with whom it deals
who, other than the individual, can access personal information, and the conditions for access
the entity’s process or schedule for updating its APP Privacy Policy, and how changes will be publicised
if the entity interacts with and collects personal information about a vulnerable segment of the community (such as children), the criteria that will be applied and the procedure that will be followed in collecting and holding that personal information
the situations in which a person can deal with the entity by not identifying themselves or by using a pseudonym (see APP 2, Chapter 2)
information retention or destruction practices or obligations specific to the entity.

APP 1 — Making an APP Privacy Policy publicly available > Making an APP Privacy Policy available free of charge and in an appropriate form
1.81 APP 1.5 requires an APP entity to take reasonable steps to make its APP Privacy Policy available free of charge and in an appropriate form. This furthers the objective of APP 1 of ensuring personal information is managed in an open and transparent way.
1.82 An APP entity is generally expected to make its policy available by publishing it on its website (see Note to APP 1.5). The information in the policy may be provided using a layered approach (see paragraph 1.12 above). The policy should be prominently displayed, accessible and easy to download. For example, a prominent link or privacy icon, displayed on each page of the entity’s website, could provide a direct link to the APP Privacy Policy. If it is foreseeable that the policy may be accessed by individuals with special needs (such as individuals with a vision impairment, or individuals from a non-English speaking background), appropriate accessibility measures should be available. Agencies are also required to comply with any applicable government or statutory accessibility requirements. [20]
1.83 Online publication may not be appropriate in some circumstances, for example, where the APP entity does not have an online presence or where individuals who regularly interact with the entity may not have internet access. In these circumstances, options an entity should consider include:
displaying the policy on a stand at the entity’s premises so it can be seen by members of the public
distributing a printout of the policy on request
including details about how to access the policy at the bottom of all correspondence to individuals
where the entity interacts with individuals by telephone, informing them during the telephone call of how the policy may be accessed in a particular form.

APP 1 — Making an APP Privacy Policy publicly available > Making an APP Privacy Policy available in a requested form
1.84 APP 1.6 requires an APP entity, upon request, to take reasonable steps to provide a person or body with a copy of its APP Privacy Policy in the form requested. This should be done as soon as reasonably practicable after the request is received.
1.85 The reference to a ‘body’ requesting a copy of a policy makes it clear that a request may be made other than by an individual or entity that is subject to the Privacy Act.
1.86 An APP entity can decline to provide a copy of its APP Privacy Policy in a particular form if it would not be reasonable in the circumstances to meet the request. The steps that are reasonable will depend upon:
other steps taken by the entity to make its policy publicly available and accessible
the practicability, including time and cost involved. However, an entity is not excused from providing a copy in a particular form by reason only that it would be inconvenient, time-consuming or impose some cost to do so. Whether these factors make it unreasonable to take a particular step will depend on whether the burden is excessive in all the circumstances
the sensitivity of the personal information held. More rigorous steps may be required where the entity holds ‘sensitive information’ (defined in s 6(1) and discussed in Chapter B (Key concepts)) or information of a sensitive nature
whether the entity has unique or unusual information handling practices
any reasons given by the body or person for requesting the policy in a particular form, and
any accessibility or other specific needs of the body or person requesting the policy. For example, it may be reasonable to provide the policy in a form that can be accessed via assistive technology where appropriate.
1.87 Inherent in the obligation to take ‘reasonable steps’ is an expectation that an APP Privacy Policy will usually be made available free of charge. The cost of doing so should be treated as part of an APP entity’s normal operating costs. If a charge is imposed, the reason for the charge and the basis of calculation should be clearly communicated and explained before the policy is made available in the requested form, and the charge should be calculated at the lowest reasonable cost.

APP 2 provides that individuals must have the option of dealing anonymously or by pseudonym with an APP entity.

Anonymity means that an individual dealing with an APP entity cannot be identified and the entity does not collect personal information or identifiers.
A pseudonym is a name, term or descriptor that is different to an individual’s actual name. Where applicable, an APP entity must ensure that individuals are made aware of their opportunity to deal anonymously or by pseudonym with the entity.

APP 2 — What does APP 2 say?
2.1 APP 2 provides that individuals must have the option of not identifying themselves, or of using a pseudonym, when dealing with an APP entity in relation to a particular matter.
2.2 That principle does not apply in relation to a particular matter if:
the APP entity is required or authorised by or under an Australian law, or a court/tribunal order, to deal with individuals who have identified themselves (APP 2.2(a)), or
it is impracticable for the APP entity to deal with individuals who have not identified themselves or used a pseudonym (APP 2.2(b)).
2.3 ‘Anonymity’ and ‘pseudonymity’ are different concepts. APP 2 requires that both options be made available to individuals dealing with an APP entity unless one of the two exceptions applies. Both options must also be made available each time an individual interacts with the entity, that is, when a person is ‘dealing with an APP entity in relation to a particular matter’ (APP 2.1). Similarly, the exceptions (‘required or authorised by law’ and ‘impracticability’) apply to the particular dealing between an individual and the entity.

APP 2 — The difference between anonymity and pseudonymity > Anonymity
2.4 Anonymity requires that an individual may deal with an APP entity without providing any personal information or identifiers. The entity should not be able to identify the individual at the time of the dealing or subsequently.
2.5 Examples of anonymous dealings include an unidentified individual telephoning an APP entity to inquire generally about its goods or services, and an individual completing a retail transaction and paying for goods in cash.

APP 2 — The difference between anonymity and pseudonymity > Pseudonymity
2.6 Pseudonymity requires that an individual may deal with an APP entity by using a name, term or descriptor that is different to the person’s actual name. Examples include an email address that does not contain the person’s actual name, a user name that a person uses when participating in an online forum, or an artist who uses a ‘pen-name’ or ‘screen-name’.
2.7 The use of a pseudonym does not necessarily mean that an individual cannot be identified. The individual may choose to divulge their identity, or to volunteer personal information necessary to implement a particular transaction, such as credit information or an address at which goods can be delivered. Similarly, an APP entity may have in place a registration system that enables a person to participate by pseudonym in a moderated online discussion forum, on condition that the person is identifiable to the forum moderator or the entity.
2.8 An APP entity should bear in mind that the object of APP 2 is to provide individuals with the opportunity to deal with the entity without revealing their identity. Personal information should only be linked to a pseudonym if this is required or authorised by law, it is impracticable for the entity to act differently, or the individual has consented to providing or linking the additional personal information. An entity could also restrict access to personal information that is linked to a pseudonym to authorised personnel (for a discussion of the security requirements for personal information, see Chapter 11 (APP 11)).
